note: This rebellion is described in 3:4–27. It also appears on the extrabiblical inscription of the Moabite Stone. King Mesha of Moab provided his version of the events of the war with Israel, and it differs with the Israelite account. The biblical narrative gives precedence to Israel’s victories over Moab, and Mesha emphasizes Moab’s advantages over Israel.
Lit. “lord of the flies”; it is perhaps a purposeful revision of the name Baal-zebul, which means “Baal is exalted.” Ahaziah, king of Israel, looks for help from this local pagan deity.

See note on 1 Kin. 17:1.

**king of Samaria.** See note on 1 Kin. 16:24.

verse_quote: a garment of hair ... a belt of leather.
note: In his appearance, his ascetic life, and his prophetic boldness, John the Baptist resembles Elijah (Matt. 3:4). Both prophets carried out a ministry of judgment and repentance (Matt. 3:1–12; Luke 3:2–17).

verse_quote: man of God, the king says, “Come down.”
note: For Ahaziah, Elijah’s prophecy constitutes interference in the affairs of state, and he should therefore be held accountable to the king for his actions. Ahaziah’s response reveals a characteristically Canaanite understanding of the unbridled powers of kingship (1 Sam. 8:11–17; 1 Kin. 21:2 note; cf. Deut. 17:14–20).

Jehoram, like Ahaziah, is a son of Ahab (3:1; 1 Kin. 22:51). This Jehoram of the northern kingdom of Israel should not be confused with Jehoram (or Joram), the son and successor to Jehoshaphat (see 8:16, 23), who reigns in the southern kingdom (Judah) at about the same time.

verse_quote: Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
note: See note on 1 Kin. 11:41.

verse_quote: up to heaven by a whirlwind.
note:
In the Bible, only Elijah and Enoch (Gen. 5:24) are privileged not to die but to be directly taken up to heaven.

**Gilgal.** Probably located at Khirbet el-Mafjar, about two miles (3 km) northeast of Jericho. It was the first place Israel camped in the land of promise during the period of the conquest (Josh. 4:19).
A major Israelite city in the central highlands (1 Kin. 12:29 note).
Prophetic communities that follow a prominent prophetic leader (4:1, 38; 6:1; 9:1).

Located at Tell es-Sultan about three miles (5 km) west of the Jordan River and ten miles (16 km) north of the Dead Sea. This was the first city conquered by Israel under the leadership of Joshua (Josh. 6).
Elijah, like Moses and Joshua before him, witnesses a division of waters that allows God’s chosen to pass through safely on dry ground (Ex. 14:21, 22; Josh. 3:14–17).

In Israel the oldest son received a double share of the family inheritance and with it the right of succession (Deut. 21:17). Elisha’s desire for “a double portion of your spirit” is therefore a bold request to be the “firstborn” heir of Elijah’s ministry.

verse_quote: You have asked a hard thing.
note: It is not up to Elijah but to God to determine whether Elisha’s daring request will be met.

verse_quote: chariots of fire and horses of fire.
note: God’s heavenly attendants escort Elijah to heaven by a whirlwind. Fire appears several times in Elijah’s ministry as a sign of God’s all-consuming power (1:10, 12, 14; 1 Kin. 18:38; cf. 1 Kin. 19:12). These chariots appear later in 6:16, 17.

This title of respect for a person of authority (Gen. 45:8; Judg. 17:10; Matt. 23:9) will later be used for Elisha (6:21; 13:14). The prophet Malachi declares that Elijah will return before the coming of the “day of the LORD” (Mal. 4:5 and note). Elijah will prepare the people for the Lord’s ministry (1:8 note).
Earlier, Elijah cast his cloak upon Elisha as a sign that Elisha would be his successor (1 Kin. 19:19). What was promised then, now takes place.

verse_quote: the water was parted ... and Elisha went over.
note: God designated Joshua as the approved successor to Moses (Num. 27:12–23; Deut. 31:1–8; 34:9; Josh. 1:1–9) by having Joshua lead the people across the Jordan River into the Promised Land, much as Moses led the people through the Red Sea (Ex. 14; 15; Josh. 3). Now God designates Elisha as the successor to Elijah by dividing the Jordan for him as He did for Elijah (v. 8).

verse_quote: the sons of the prophets ... bowed to the ground before him.
note: See note on 1 Kin. 20:35.
These men are probably the leaders of Jericho (v. 18).

A new vessel will be free from any ceremonial pollution.

**put salt in it.** Salt is a preservative and therefore an appropriate symbol for how God is faithful to His promises and maintains His people (Lev. 2:13; Num. 18:19; 2 Chr. 13:5; Ezek. 43:24; Matt. 5:13; Mark 9:49, 50).
It may be that the youths were sarcastically comparing Elisha to his teacher Elijah, who wore a garment made of hair (1:8), and taunting him to “go up” to heaven as Elijah did (v. 11).

Elisha in his ministry is characteristically compassionate toward the repentant and hard on the unresponsive and obstinate. The mauling of the Bethel youths becomes another public manifestation of the power of God present in His spokesman Elisha (vv. 14, 21).

verse_quote: In the eighteenth year of Jehosh­aphat.
note:
Jehoram of Judah and his father, Jehoshaphat, probably rule together as co-regents for approximately five years (853–848 B.C.). If so, “the second year of Jehoram” (1:17) is the same as “the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat” (3:1).

**twelve years.** 852–841 B.C.

See note on 1 Kin. 14:23. Jehoram initiates a minor reform, attempting to undo some of the damage of his parents. Ahab’s reign was particularly heinous; Jehoram is evil but not to the degree of his predecessors.
See note on 1 Kin. 12:30. Jehoram’s reform is not thoroughgoing; he does not address the fundamental flaw in the worship of the northern kingdom.

According to the Moabite Stone, Mesha acknowledges that, like his predecessors, he also is a vassal to Israel. He claims to have freed his land from subjection to Israel and boasts that “Israel has perished forever.”

**he had to deliver to the king.** Part of Mesha’s obligations as a vassal are to pay tribute regularly to his superior.
The ruler of Edom is likely a vassal to the king of Judah and therefore obliged to assist him (cf. 8:20; 1 Kin. 22:47).

verse_quote: Is there no prophet of the LORD here.
note: Jehoshaphat earlier posed a similar question to Ahab (1 Kin. 22:7).
Elisha consents to prophesy for the coalition but only for the sake of Jehoshaphat, whose reign is viewed positively (1 Kin. 22:43).

The musician is employed to provide an atmosphere suitable for the reception of divine revelation (cf. 1 Sam. 10:5, 6).

**the hand of the** LORD**.** A metaphor for God’s power. Though it is frequently used to describe God’s power in judgment against an enemy (Ex. 9:3; 1 Sam. 5:6) or His people (Deut. 2:15; Ruth 1:13), it can also refer to God’s power enabling His servants to receive and proclaim revelation (Ezek. 1:3; 37:1).
This is usually identified as the Valley of Zered, a wadi that flows into the southern end of the Dead Sea and forms the border between Edom and Moab (Deut. 2:13).

verse_quote: water came from the direction of Edom.
note: Flash floods in the mountains of Edom flow rapidly through the stream bed in the direction of the Dead Sea.

verse_quote: the water ... as red as blood.
note: The water is colored by Edom’s red sandstone (cf. Gen. 25:30).

Probably this is the capital of Moab (Is. 16:7, 11; Jer. 48:31, 36), about eleven miles (18 km) east of the Dead Sea and fourteen miles (23 km) north of the Valley of Zered, which is at the southern tip of the Dead Sea.

This grisly act is meant to induce the god Chemosh to deliver the Moabites from certain defeat. Child sacrifice is expressly forbidden in Israel (Ex. 34:20; Deut. 18:10); nevertheless, two later kings of Judah (Ahaz and Manasseh) apparently practice it (16:3; 21:6).

See note on 1 Kin. 20:35.

**my two children to be his slaves.** The Mosaic law allows taking children as bond-servants (or slaves) for a limited period of time (Ex. 21:2, 7; Lev. 25:39–46; Deut. 15:12–18). Unfortunately, this provision was often abused (Neh. 5:5–8; Jer. 34:8–22; Amos 2:6; 8:6). Such situations fall under the rights of redemption (Lev. 25:23–55; cf. Ruth 4:1–12). Apparently, this widow has no kinsman-redeemer to act on her behalf, and thus she seeks Elisha’s intervention.
Shunem is located at the confluence of the Jezreel and Esdraelon valleys (1 Kin. 1:3 note).
Elisha’s personal attendant (5:20–27; 6:15).

verse_quote: a word spoken on your behalf.
note: This woman is to be contrasted with the widow of 4:1–7. She is married, wealthy, and among her own people; the widow has few of those advantages.

verse_quote: she has no son, and her husband is old.
note: An heir is of great importance because the family name and possessions are passed on to the children. Without a son, a family’s home and goods are given to others. Moreover, living as a widow, a real prospect for this woman, will very difficult (1 Kin. 17:9 note).

Throughout the Bible, God’s grace to childless women, such as Sarah (Gen. 17:16–19), Rebekah (Gen. 25:21–26), Rachel (Gen. 29:31; 30:22–24), and Elizabeth (Luke 1:5–25), shows His love and compassion for the those in need.

She refuses to accept the death of her son and conceals his body in Elisha’s room so that the ritual of mourning will not begin (Gen. 50:10; 2 Chr. 35:25; Job 2:12, 13; Mark 5:38; John 11:33).

**man of God.** A term for a prophet, not a way of saying “a godly man.”

verse_quote: It is neither new moon nor Sabbath.
note: Ancient Israel had a lunar calendar, and a festival was celebrated at each new moon (Num. 10:10; 28:11–15; Ezra 3:5; Neh. 10:33; Is. 1:13, 14; Amos 8:5). The law does not permit work on the Sabbath and possibly not on the new moon either (Ex. 16:23; 20:8–10; 1 Sam. 20:5; 1 Chr. 23:31).

A sign of respect (John 11:32).

**the LORD has hidden it.** Elisha is surprised by the news; prophets are not all-knowing or all-seeing but are dependent on God’s revelation to them.

See note on 2:1.

**a famine.** Often due to Israel’s disobedience (Lev. 26:18–20).

**Set on the large pot.** During a famine, Elisha’s request is not trivial (cf. 1 Kin. 17:11–13).
There exist in this area several more or less poisonous gourds that resemble edible plants.

In the hill country of Ephraim, on the Brook of Kanah.

**bread of the firstfruits.** By bringing the firstfruits of the harvest, the man shows his dedication to Elisha and his gratitude for his prophetic work (Lev. 2:14; 23:9–21; Deut. 18:3–5).

This king and the king of Israel (v. 5) are probably Ben-hadad II (8:7; 13:3; 1 Kin. 20:1) and Jehoram (1:17; 3:1; 9:24), respectively.

**leper.** Heb. “a skin disease,” which can refer a variety of skin ailments, including leprosy (Hansen’s disease). See Lev. 13, 14.
During the long history of tension between Israel and Syria, there have often been skirmishes and raids along the border.

verse_quote: a letter to the king of Israel.
note:
The Syrian king sends an official letter to the king of Israel introducing Naaman and asking for a favor on his behalf. The Syrian king has mistakenly supposed that Elisha’s work is at the command of the Israelite king.

**ten talents of silver, six thousand shekels of gold.** That is, about 750 pounds (340 kg) of silver and 150 pounds (68 kg) of gold.
A sign of great distress (1 Kin. 21:27 note). The king of Israel is alarmed that he is under obligation to cure the leper.

verse_quote: Why have you torn your clothes.
note:
Elisha scolds the king for reacting to the Syrian request with such alarm and not believing that God can help him.

**he may know that there is a prophet in Israel.** See 3:11; 8:7, 8; 1 Kin. 17:24; 18:36. Elisha responds affirmatively to the Syrian gesture (v. 3).

Both Elijah and Elisha often test the faith of the people to whom they ministered (1 Kin. 17:13; 2 Kin. 4:3, 4). In this case, Elisha does not even meet with Naaman but sends instructions through a messenger.

verse_quote: wave his hand over the place.
note: Not realizing the importance of divine freedom and the critical role of faith, Naaman thinks there is something contemptible about having to bathe seven times in the river.

verse_quote: Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus.
note: If the prophetic healing is a meaningless ritual, Naaman might as well stay at home. Naaman displays his national pride as he scorns the Jordan River in comparison to the rivers of Syria.

verse_quote: there is no God in all the earth but in Israel.
note: Naaman is not merely saying that the Lord is more powerful than the Syrian gods; he is confessing that there is only one God, the Lord. In saying this, Naaman adopts the faith of Israel as his own (1 Kin. 18:39).
The words are an oath (1 Kin. 1:17 note).

People in the ancient Near East believed that the gods were tied to the lands they ruled. Naaman asks for dirt from the Lord’s land to sanctify the altar he plans to build for Him in another country. (cf. Ex. 20:24, 25).
Lit. “pomegranate”; a parody of the name Ramanu, the Syrian storm god corresponding to Baal. This chief deity of Syria is also known by the name Hadad (Zech. 12:11).
See note on 1 Kin. 20:35.
Refers not to coins (which are probably not yet in use in this era) but to quantities of gold or silver.

verse_quote: to you and to your descendants.
note: Sin is not only individual but also corporate (Ex. 20:5). It is ironic justice that Gehazi will not benefit from Naaman’s cure but will receive Naaman’s disease.
See note on 1 Kin. 20:35.
Heb. “iron.” Apparently, iron was a rare commodity in ancient Israel (1 Sam. 13:19–21); thus, this tool was rare and expensive.

As in ch. 5, the kings of Syria and Israel (v. 9) are unnamed. They are most likely Ben-hadad II (8:7; 13:3; 1 Kin. 20:1) and Jehoram (1:17; 3:1; 9:24).

**warring against Israel.** Despite the ratification of a treaty between Israel and Syria (1 Kin. 20:34; 22:1), the two nations continue to fight.
Elisha intervenes to warn the king of Israel of the Syrian plans, not because of Jehoram’s good behavior but because he is a watchman for Israel. He does his duty to protect the covenant people.

This town is located approximately nine miles (14 km) due north of Samaria, the capital city of Israel. Syrian penetration this far into Israel is quite ominous. Excavations at the site have uncovered an extensive settlement from the ninth and eighth centuries B.C..

Elisha is referring to God’s heavenly host or army (cf. Josh. 5:13–15; 2 Chr. 32:7, 8; Dan. 10:20; 12:1). In fighting wars for God, the Israelites believe that they are fighting with the power of God (Ex. 15:1–12; Deut. 20:1–4; 2 Sam. 22:7–16, 31–51). See also Matt. 26:53.

Elisha prays that the servant will see something that does not appear to the naked eye: God’s heavenly armies waiting to do battle with the Syrians.

**behold, the mountain was full.** In v. 15, the Syrian army surrounds the city of Dothan with horses and chariots. Here the horses and chariots of the Lord surround Elisha on every side.
In an ironic fashion, Elisha prays that the Syrians will become blind, whereas in the previous verse he prayed that his servant’s eyes would see.
The kings call Elisha “father” by way of respect (2:12 note; 13:14).
Elisha’s point is twofold. First, the captives do not belong to the king, because the victory is God’s. Second, captives at the mercy of their captors are not normally killed (Deut. 20:11).
Most likely Ben-hadad II (8:7; 1 Kin. 20:1 note).

verse_quote: a donkey’s head was sold for eighty shekels of silver.
note: An undesirable part of an unclean animal (Lev. 11:2–7; Deut. 14:4–8) is selling for two pounds (1 kg) of silver.

verse_quote: Give your son, that we may eat him.
note: The curses of the Sinai covenant envision exactly this sort of cannibalism (Lev. 26:29; Deut. 28:52–57; cf. Lam. 2:20; 4:10; Ezek. 5:10).

A sign of distress (1 Kin. 21:27 note).

**he had sackcloth beneath on his body.** It becomes known that even the king is in a state of mourning (Gen. 37:34; 1 Kin. 21:27; Jon. 3:5, 6).

verse_quote: the elders were sitting with him.
note: The leaders of the city are conferring with Elisha, not with the king (1 Kin. 8:1 note).

verse_quote: a seah of fine flour shall be sold for a shekel.
note:
Elisha prophesies a sudden reversal of the famine; seven quarts (6.6 L) of flour will sell for less than one-half ounce (14 g) of silver (cf. 6:25).

**at the gate of Samaria.** The city gate in antiquity was an important place for the economic and political activity of a town. The gate is where the elders congregated (Ruth 4:1, 2), and much trade and other business occurred there.
The commander is mocking the situation by disparaging God’s work in the turn of events from little to plenty.

verse_quote: at the entrance to the gate.
note: The Mosaic regulations prohibit people with skin diseases from living in the community (Lev. 13:46; Num. 5:1–4; 12:14, 15).

The Hittites live in Asia Minor (Num. 13:29). Here the Syrian army may confuse Egypt (Heb. _misrayim_) with a minor state next to the Hittites, the name of which is similar to the Hebrew name for Egypt (cf. 1 Kin. 10:28, 29 notes).
The writer does not state how much time has elapsed between the events of ch. 4 and this incident.

verse_quote: in the land of the Philistines.
note: On the southwestern plain, where rainfall was quite adequate for agriculture. It was a common place for ancient peoples to seek refuge during times of famine, as did the patriarch Isaac (Gen. 26:1).
In his capacity as overseer of the nation’s judicial system, the king hears special cases (1 Kin. 3:16 note). Apparently, someone absconded with the woman’s holdings while she was in Philistia.

He is unnamed, but if this king is Jehoram (1:17; 3:13), it is surprising that he knows nothing of Elisha’s activities. Either this incident takes place soon after the events of 4:8–37, or the king referred to here is Jehu (ch. 9).

**Gehazi.** Elisha’s personal attendant who had been struck with leprosy (4:12 note; 5:27 note).

It is unusual for Israel’s prophets to visit foreign capitals, but Elisha is on an unusual mission: to implement the first of the three commands God gave to Elijah on Mount Horeb (1 Kin. 19:15, 16).

**Ben-hadad.** Probably Ben-hadad II (6:24; 1 Kin. 20:1 note).
The Lord told Elijah to anoint Hazael as the king over Syria as part of God’s judgment against the house of Ahab (1 Kin. 19:15).

verse_quote: all kinds of goods of Damascus.
note:
The city of Damascus has an international reputation as a trade center in Elisha’s era.

**Your son Ben-hadad.** This is a diplomatic indication of the high regard Ben-hadad has for Elisha (6:21; 13:14).

Some observe that the Hebrew “to him” can also be translated “not.” The text would therefore read, “you shall certainly not recover.” The reason Elisha will know this is that “the LORD has shown” him that truth. On the other hand, if read simply as “you shall certainly recover,” one can conclude that perhaps Elisha is attempting to deceive the king of Syria. The monarch will be duped into a false sense of security and be unprepared for Hazael’s attack.
Such atrocities were common in ancient wars (Ps. 137:9; Is. 13:16; Hos. 10:14; 13:16; Amos 1:13; Nah. 3:10). Elisha does not approve of such actions; he mourns them.

This expression of self-deprecation before a superior occurs in a number of extrabiblical documents (the Lachish letters) from early sixth-century Judah (see also a similar formula in 1 Sam. 17:43; 24:14; 2 Sam. 3:8). Assyrian inscriptions refer to Hazael as “the son of a nobody,” that is, a commoner.
Hazael takes Elisha’s prophecy as a license to commit murder, an indication of Hazael’s ruthlessness.

Jehoram probably reigned together with his father, Jehoshaphat, for five years before becoming the sole monarch of Judah (1:17; 1 Kin. 22:42). This verse marks the death of Jehoshaphat and the beginning of Jehoram’s (Joram’s) independent rule (848–841 B.C.).

verse_quote: walked in the way of the kings of Israel.
note:
Usually Judah’s kings are evaluated with reference to their predecessors. Jehoram is purposely compared to the “house of Ahab” because he imitates their policies. Ahab introduced and sanctioned Baal worship in the northern kingdom of Israel, and now Jehoram does the same in Judah.

**the daughter of Ahab.** The ruling dynasties of north and south are now linked by ideology and by blood (v. 26; 2 Chr. 21:6). Athaliah promotes Baal worship in the south, much as her mother, Jezebel, promoted Baal religion in the north (1 Kin. 16:31; 18:4; 19:2).

verse_quote: for the sake of David his servant.
note:
Because of God’s love for David, He is longsuffering with Judah (2 Sam. 7:12–16 notes; 1 Kin. 11:4 note).

**give a lamp ... forever.** See notes on 2 Sam. 21:17 and 1 Kin. 11:36.

See note on 1 Kin. 8:8.

**Libnah revolted.** Libnah is near the border with Philistia, about fifteen miles (24 km) southeast of Ashdod. It was conquered by Joshua (Josh. 10:29, 30) and designated a Levitical city (Josh. 21:13). Libnah revolts because Jehoram has apostatized and led Judah astray.

verse_quote: Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
note: See note on 1 Kin. 11:41.
As king of Judah, he should not be confused with his maternal uncle King Ahaziah of Israel (1 Kin. 22:40, 51; 2 Kin. 1:18).

verse_quote: twelfth year of Joram the son of Ahab.

note: See note on v. 18.

verse_quote: He also walked in the way of the house of Ahab and did what was evil.
note: Like his father, Jehoram, Ahaziah imitates the religious policies of Ahab, sanctioning in Judah the worship of the Canaanite god Baal (1 Kin. 16:31 note).

verse_quote: He went with Joram the son of Ahab to make war.
note: Earlier Jehoshaphat of Judah aligned himself with Ahab of Israel in a campaign against the Syrians at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kin. 22). This campaign, like the earlier one, ends in disaster (1 Kin. 22:32–37).

verse_quote: King Joram returned to be healed in Jezreel.
note:
A royal residence for the northern kings was maintained at Jezreel (1 Kin. 18:45 note). It is also the site of Ahab and Jezebel’s horrendous crime against Naboth (1 Kin. 21).

**Ramah.** That is, Ramoth-gilead.

See note on 1 Kin. 20:35.

**Tie up your garments.** So that the son of the prophet can travel quickly (1 Kin. 18:46; 2 Kin. 4:29).

verse_quote: take ... oil and pour it on his head.
note:
Elisha directs one of the prophets to perform a ritual of anointing used to designate a (future) king (11:12; 23:30; 1 Sam. 9:16; 10:1; 16:13; 2 Sam. 2:7).

**flee.** Why Elisha commands the son of the prophet to run immediately after he anoints Jehu is perhaps due to Jehu’s reputation as a rash and ruthless person (see v. 20).
Part of the Lord’s vengeance on the house of Ahab is due to the killing of many true prophets by Jezebel (1 Kin. 18:4, 13).

verse_quote: like the house of Jeroboam ... like the house of Baasha.
note: God destroyed these two earlier Israelite dynasties due to their unfaithfulness (1 Kin. 15:27–30; 16:8–13).
The lack of a burial is a sign of disgrace (Jer. 8:2; 16:4–6; 22:19; 25:33). This is a fulfillment of the prophecy of 1 Kin. 21:23.
Because of their unusual lifestyle, eccentric habits, and ecstatic prophetic messages, the ancient prophets struck some people as deranged (cf. Jer. 29:26; Hos. 9:7).

This sign of the new king is reminiscent of Jesus’ triumphal entry (Matt. 21:8).

**they blew the trumpet.** The trumpets announce the anointing of a king (cf. 2 Sam. 15:10; 1 Kin. 1:34).
Jehu’s coup reaches its climax at the very place Ahab and Jezebel had Naboth killed (1 Kin. 21:1–16).
Jehu’s question addresses the heart of the issue. There can be no true peace where there is idolatry and witchcraft (cf. 17:17; 21:6; Judg. 2:17; 8:33; Hos. 2; 3; Nah. 3:4).

verse_quote: the LORD made this pronouncement against him.
Ahaziah the king of Judah ... died.
note:
Jehu is not authorized to kill the descendants of David who are related to the house of Ahab through his daughter Athaliah (cf. vv. 8–10). Jehu is too zealous in carrying out his commission. Hosea criticizes him for “the blood of Jezreel” (Hos. 1:4).

**Megiddo.** A prominent Israelite city of the time. Ahab built extensive structures here, such as a massive water tunnel and a series of tripartite pillared buildings that served as either stables or storehouses.
This figure may count only the whole years of his reign, leaving out the year he took the throne. This would agree with the figures given in 8:25, 26.
Again the scene of action ominously returns to the site of Naboth’s murder.
In referring to Jehu in this way, Jezebel is sarcastically alluding to Zimri’s bloody purge almost half a century earlier (1 Kin. 16:9–15).

This word can refer to men who were employed as guards and attendants of royal harems in the ancient Near East (as here) or to officials who served in the royal court (20:18; Is. 39:7; Jer. 29:2; 34:19; 38:7; Dan. 1:3, 7–10).
Jehu does not dignify Jezebel with the title “queen of Israel,” but refers to her as the daughter of Ethbaal, the Sidonian king (1 Kin. 16:31).

verse_quote: dogs shall eat the flesh of Jezebel.
note: The judgment oracle Jezebel so contemptuously scorned in her life is now fulfilled in her death (1 Kin. 21:23). Dogs were also present at Ahab’s death (1 Kin. 22:38).

This figure probably includes grandsons. How many wives Ahab had is not known, though we know he had several (1 Kin. 20:5).

**elders.** See note on 1 Kin. 8:1.

**guardians of the sons.** These guardians are responsible for bringing up and educating children in the royal household. The king is dead, and Jehu addresses various lesser figures.
Jehu is forcing the issue. Will those who have been most loyal to Ahab and his house continue to support them?

See note on 1 Kin. 4:6.

**over the city.** This position is similar to the governor of the city in 1 Kin. 22:26.

verse_quote: take the heads of your master’s sons.
note: Jehu’s demand takes the form of a pun. In Hebrew “head” can mean part of the body or it can mean “leader” or “chief.” It is uncertain whether Jehu is asking for the death of all Ahab’s male descendants or for the leaders among the royal princes.

The leaders of Samaria take no chances; they carry out Jehu’s command literally. In this way another component of Elijah’s prophecy comes to pass (1 Kin. 21:21–24). This drastic action is not unknown in the ancient Near East: its purpose was to wipe out any descendant that might seek retribution at a later time.
Assyrian kings, such as Ashurbanipal II and Shalmaneser III, intimidated populations by leaving heaps of heads by the city gates.
Jehu’s actions go far beyond the mandate of Elijah’s oracle (1 Kin. 21:21–24) and the oracle delivered personally to Jehu (9:7–10).
These relatives do not realize that a coup has taken place. Thus Jehu attempts to exterminate not only the descendants of the king of Israel but also the descendants of the king of Judah.

He is from a family or clan in Israel that leads a life of austerity and abstinence. In keeping with their convictions about worshiping God, the Rechabites do not plant fields or drink wine (Jer. 35).

verse_quote: Ahab served Baal a little, but Jehu will serve him much.
note: Jehu’s ruse is designed to entice Baal supporters to reveal their allegiance publicly. Having utterly destroyed the house of Ahab (v. 17), Jehu now begins his purge of Baal worship in Israel.
Ahab built this structure in Samaria (1 Kin. 16:32).

See note on 1 Kin. 14:23.

**burned it.** Stone monuments can be shattered by heating them with fire and then pouring cold water on them.
This desecrates the site and discourages any future Baal worshipers from trying to rebuild their temple.

Although Jehu wipes out Baal worship from the northern kingdom, he does not restore or implement orthodoxy in Israel. He continues the idolatry of Jeroboam in regard to the golden calf worship (1 Kin. 12:25–30).
LORD**.** On the importance of keeping the law, see note on 1 Kin. 2:3.

This attack has been confirmed through excavation: Sennacherib built a siege ramp at the southwestern part of the city in order to penetrate the city’s defense with siege machines. The Judean defenders responded by building a counter-siege ramp to strengthen their defenses at that point. Both of these ramps have been uncovered.

Sennacherib’s annals consistently report that Sennacherib not only demanded tribute from kings who “did not bow in submission to my yoke,” but also insisted on deposing such rebellious kings and replacing them with monarchs of his own choosing. It is to serve as a sign to Hezekiah that nature is at God’s beck and call, and thus that the Lord controls even sickness that leads to death.

Merodach-baladan was king over Babylon from 721 B.C. until he was forced by the Assyrian King Sargon II into a vassal relationship in 710 B.C.. Shortly after Sargon’s death (705 B.C.), Merodach-baladan led his country to a short-lived independence in 704 B.C. before Sennacherib defeated him in 703 B.C. (v. 1 note).

verse_quote: his armory, all that was found in his storehouses.
note: This display probably occurs before Hezekiah sends his treasures as tribute to the Assyrians (v. 1 note; 18:14–16 note). Hezekiah is attempting to impress his Babylonian visitors with his nation’s wealth and power. Hezekiah is receptive to the idea of an alignment with Egypt and Babylon. Isaiah opposed Ahaz’s treaty with Assyria (Is. 7:1–17), and he opposes this attempt to make a treaty with Babylon and Egypt (vv. 16–18; Is. 30; 31).

Isaiah rebukes a naive Hezekiah. The same treasures that might induce a treaty might also attract an invasion. This prophecy is fulfilled by a Babylonian invasion in 598 B.C. and by the Babylonian exile of 586 B.C. Having sought refuge with the Babylonians, Hezekiah discovers that the Babylonians will ultimately be Judah’s ruin.

verse_quote: your own sons, who shall be born to you.
note:

**eunuchs.** See note on 9:32.

verse_quote: the pool and the conduit and brought water into the city.
note:
Hezekiah made improvements in Jerusalem’s water supply in advance of the Assyrian invasion. An inscription in the Siloam Tunnel celebrates the completion of an impressive engineering feat. The conduit runs from the Gihon spring outside the city wall (cf. 1 Kin. 1:33 note) through seventeen hundred feet of solid rock to the Pool of Siloam inside the city.

**Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.** See note on 1 Kin. 11:41.

These verses summarize the evil reign of Manasseh, king of Judah. Manasseh leads Judah into sin by reintroducing idolatry; he is also guilty of shedding innocent blood (v. 16). So great is Manasseh’s sin that God pronounces disaster on Judah and Jerusalem. While the parallel account of Manasseh’s life in 2 Chr. 33 highlights his shortcomings, it also reveals that he later repents of his sins.

**fifty-five years.** That is, 697–642 B.C. Some scholars suggest that Hezekiah died in 686 B.C. If they are correct, Manassah served as co-regent with Hezekiah for ten years as king of Judah and reigned forty-five years after Hezekiah died. In any case, Manasseh’s reign is the longest of any Judean king. Assyrian records say that Manasseh was a vassal of both Esarhaddon (681–669 B.C.) and Ashurbanipal (669–627 B.C.).

Manasseh presides over the worst period of infidelity in Judah’s history. The reforms instituted by Hezekiah are reversed by his son. Manasseh also introduces pagan elements into Judean worship that have no precedent in the history of monarchy before him (vv. 3–11 notes).

verse_quote: the high places that Hezekiah his father had destroyed.
note:
See 18:4 and note on 1 Kin. 3:2.

**Asherah.** See note on 1 Kin. 14:15.

LORD**.** These altars are dedicated to “the host of heaven” (v. 5).

That promise was fulfilled during Solomon’s reign, and God blessed the temple as the divinely ordained place for sacrifice and prayer (1 Kin. 9:1–3; cf. Deut. 12:5).

Further information on Zedekiah’s reign can be found in Jer. 21; 24; 27; 29; 32; 37–39; Ezek. 17:11–21.

note: Despite being a vassal appointed by Nebuchadnezzar, Zedekiah plots with Egypt and other nations against the Babylonians (Jer. 27:3–8; Ezek. 17:11–21). Zedekiah’s ill-fated decision to rebel against Babylon is likely prompted by the encouragement of Pharaoh Hophra (Apries), who comes to power in 589 B.C.

Probably January 588 B.C. Nebuchadnezzar, before the siege of Jerusalem, attacked outlying cities. Further evidence for this comes from the site of Lachish, where twenty-one Hebrew ostraca (pieces of pottery with writing on them) have been discovered. These are addressed to an official at Lachish from a Judean officer at an outlying post. The letters were written just before the Babylonian siege of Lachish (589/588 B.C.). One contains a warning of a prophet regarding a coming assault.
The precise chronology of the siege of Jerusalem is a topic of debate. Most commentators agree that the city fell in July 586 B.C., though July 587 has also been suggested (Jer. 39:2; 52:5–7).
During the siege, Jerusalem experiences terrible privation (Jer. 38:2, 3; Lam. 4:10).

note:
Blinding was a common punishment in the ancient Near East for rebellious captives (Ezek. 12:13).

**took him to Babylon.** Zedekiah ignores the counsel of Jeremiah, who urged the king to surrender to Babylon because the Lord’s judgment was inevitable (Jer. 38:14–28). Through a peaceful surrender, Jerusalem could have been spared destruction. Zedekiah’s stubborn resistance brings only horrible results for both his family and the nation. Zedekiah himself dies in Babylon (Jer. 52:11).
Probably August 586 B.C. See note on 25:2.

The terrible carnage and destruction are deliberate. Nebuchadnezzar does not rebuild Judah with Jerusalem as a Bab­ylonian provincial capital. And unlike the Assyrians in their dealings with Israel (17:24–31; Ezra 4:2), he does not import new settlers from other areas to replace the dead and exiled.
Evidence for the destruction has been found in excavations of the city: at the base of one of the fortification towers was found a destruction layer containing Babylonian arrowheads.

Apparently, some of the people gave their allegiance to the Babylonians even before the final siege. The Babylonians took them to Babylon.

**carried into exile.** The Babylonians implement a second deportation (24:12–16), leaving only the poor to till the land (v. 12).

The Babylonian forces eliminate all the remaining leaders, not all of whom are soldiers.

Having abolished the monarchy, Nebuchadnezzar appoints Gedaliah, a well-known citizen of Judah, as governor to bring stability to the land (Jer. 40:9–12). Gedaliah’s father, Ahikam, supported Jeremiah (Jer. 26:24)..

**Ahikam.** Gedaliah’s father was a close advisor of Josiah (22:12).
Gedaliah lives in Mizpah, eight miles (13 km) north of Jerusalem (Jer. 40:6).
See note on 1 Kin. 1:17.

Possibly October 586 B.C.

**Ishmael ... of the royal family.** Ishmael’s grandfather Elishama was royal secretary under Jehoiakim (Jer. 36:12; 41:1). Ishmael is part of a faction in Judah that views Gedaliah as a collaborator and wants to resist the Babylonians (see the detailed account in Jer. 40:13–41:18). Ishmael probably has set his sights on reestablishing the throne of Judah with himself as king.

**struck down Gedaliah.** This action creates even worse conditions in Judah (Jer. 44:1–14). The exiles consider Gedaliah’s death a great loss. They institute fast days to mourn his death as well as the destruction of Judah and Jerusalem (Zech. 7:5; 8:19).

Fearing reprisals from the Babylonians, these coup leaders seek refuge in Egypt, where an anti-Babylonian pharaoh rules (24:20 note). The law of the king in Deut. 17:14–20 forbids any king in Israel to lead the people back to Egypt (Deut. 17:16). Ironically, these coup leaders in their quest for power enact one of the curses of the covenant—returning to Egypt, the land of bondage and slavery (Deut. 28:68).

The writer of Kings ends his work on a hopeful note by calling attention to the mercy shown to Jehoiachin, king of Judah, while in exile in Babylon.

**25:27 in the thirty-seventh year.** March 561 B.C.

**Evil-merodach ... began to reign.** Evil-merodach is the son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar (24:1 note).

**freed Jehoiachin ... from prison.** Administrative texts from Babylonia mention payment of rations in oil and barley to Jehoiachin, king of Judah, and five of his sons. Evil-merodach may have initiated this act of mercy on the occasion of his enthronement.

Deut. 4:25–31; 30:1–10 and King Solomon’s temple prayer (1 Kin. 8:46–53) all address conditions of exile. These texts urge repentance (Deut. 4:30; 30:2; 1 Kin. 8:47). Solomon’s prayer that the exiles might find compassion at the hands of their captors is realized in the kind treatment of Jehoiachin. Deut. 30:3–5 promises restoration to the people of God, and in 538 B.C. the Jews are allowed to return home (Ezra 1:1–4; Is. 44:24–28; 45:1–6).

verse_quote: he dined regularly at the king’s table.
note: See note on 1 Kin. 2:7. The preferential treatment of Jehoiachin is a glimmer of hope for the continuance of the promises to David (2 Sam. 7:8–16). The somber final chapters of Kings emphasize the divine judgment on Judah (21:10–15; 23:26, 27; 24:3, 4, 20; 25:21), but they also reveal in the last few verses that the destruction of Judah and Jerusalem does not cut off the line of David. There is reason to look to the future with trust in God that He will one day reestablish the Davidic dynasty. This is fulfilled through Jesus Christ, the son of David (Matt. 1:1).
